parole.testo: Probably from Latin -icus and Ancient Greek -ικός (-ikós) under influence of -cký, a variant of -ský. Some uses can be analyzed as -ika + -cký (compare Russian -и́ческий (-íčeskij)). Cognates include French -ique, English -ic, Italian -ico and Spanish -ico.

parole.significato: -ine (suffix used to form names of chemical substances)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin -īnus, from Ancient Greek -ινος (-inos).
Learned borrowing from Latin -ismus, borrowed from Ancient Greek -ῐσμός (-ĭsmós).
Borrowed from Latin -ista.

parole.significato: -ite forms nouns denoting followers or adherents of a specified person, idea, doctrine, movement, etc.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin -ītēs, from Ancient Greek -ῑ́της (-ī́tēs).
Borrowed from New Latin -itidem, from Ancient Greek -ῖτις (-îtis, “pertaining to”).

parole.significato: atmosphere (the gases surrounding the Earth or any astronomical body)
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin atmosphaera, from Ancient Greek ἀτμός (atmós, “steam”) + σφαῖρα (sphaîra, “sphere”).
Borrowed from Latin aura, from Ancient Greek αὔρα (aúra).
Learned borrowing from Latin asbestos.

parole.significato: Baptist (member of a Baptist church or denomination)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin baptista, from Ancient Greek βαπτιστής (baptistḗs). First attested in the 19th century.

parole.significato: A son of Noah and the brother of Japheth and Shem.
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Czech Chám, borrowed from Latin Chām.

parole.significato: elegy (mournful or plaintive poem or song)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin elegia (“elegy”), from Ancient Greek ἐλεγεία (elegeía).

parole.significato: ellipse (curve resulting from stretching a circle along a particular dimension)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ellīpsis.

Borrowed from Latin oesophagitis, from Ancient Greek οἰσοφάγος (oisophágos) and -itida (“-itis”).

parole.significato: pharaoh (the supreme ruler of Ancient Egypt)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Czech faraon, farao, derived from Late Latin Pharaō, Pharaōnem, from Ancient Greek φαραώ (pharaṓ), from Hebrew פַּרְעֹה (par‘ōh), from Egyptian pr-ꜥꜣ (“great house”), pr:aA
Borrowed from Latin galaxiās, from Ancient Greek γαλαξίας (galaxías, “milky”), from γάλα (gála, “milk”).

parole.significato: geography (study of the physical structure and inhabitants of the Earth)
parole.testo: From Latin geōgraphia, from Ancient Greek γεωγραφία (geōgraphía). By surface analysis, geo- + -grafie.

parole.significato: gumma, a non-cancerous growth resulting from the tertiary stage of syphilis
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin gumma (“gum”) (sticky substance from some plants), from Latin gummi (“gum”), from Ancient Greek κόμμι (kómmi, “gum”), probably from Egyptian qmy (“anointing oil”), qmyt (“acanthus resin, gum”).

parole.significato: gum, a sticky substance from some plants

From Latin hymēn (“hymen”), from Ancient Greek ὑμήν (humḗn, “skin; membrane”).

Borrowed from Latin hypotheca (“pledge for a loan”). Ultimately from Ancient Greek ὑποθήκη (hupothḗkē, “warning, pledge”), from the verb ὑποτίθημι (hupotíthēmi, “put down, pledge”).

parole.significato: idea (that which exists in the mind as the result of mental activity)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin idea, from Ancient Greek ἰδέα (idéa), from εἴδω (eídō).
Borrowed from Latin encaustum.

From Latin catapulta, from Ancient Greek καταπέλτης (katapéltēs).

Borrowed from Latin corōna. Doublet of koruna.

From late Latin lēthargia, from Ancient Greek ληθαργία (lēthargía, “drowsiness”), from λήθαργος (lḗthargos, “forgetful, lethargic”). This is a compound of λήθη (lḗthē, “oblivion”) and ἀργός (argós, “idle”), which consists of negative prefix ἀ- (a-) and noun ἔργον (érgon, “deed, work”).
Learned borrowing from Latin lochia, from Ancient Greek λοχεία (lokheía), neuter plural of λοχείος (lokheíos, “of childbirth”), from λόχος (lókhos, “childbirth”).
Borrowed from Latin lyra (“a lyre, a lyric”), from Ancient Greek λύρᾱ (lúrā, “a lyre”).

Via Latin, from Ancient Greek πρόσθεσις (prósthesis, “addition”).

parole.significato: Pygmy, pygmy (member of one of various Ancient Equatorial African tribal peoples, notable for their very short stature)
parole.testo: From Latin Pygmaeī, from Ancient Greek πυγμαῖος (pugmaîos, “a member of a race of dwarves”), from πυγμή (pugmḗ, “fist (as small as a fist)”).
Derived from Latin podium, from Ancient Greek πόδιον (pódion, “base”), from diminutive of πούς (poús, “foot”).

Derived from Latin spira, from Ancient Greek σπεῖρα (speîra).

parole.significato: stigma (an indication of infamy or disgrace)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin stigma, from Ancient Greek στίγμα (stígma, “mark of slavery or disgrace”).
Borrowed from Latin symbolum.

Borrowed from Latin thema, from Ancient Greek θέμα (théma).

parole.significato: zone (area distinguished on the basis of a particular characteristic)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin zōna, from Ancient Greek ζώνη (zṓnē). Related to pás. First attested in the 19th century.
Inherited from Old Czech diábel, from Latin diabolus, from Ancient Greek διάβολος (diábolos).

parole.significato: stole (priest's garment, a stripe of cloth worn around the neck and shoulders)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Czech štóla, from Latin stola (“stola”), from Ancient Greek στολή (stolḗ), which is from Ancient Greek στέλλω (stéllō).
Inherited from Old Czech žák, from Ecclesiastical Latin diācus, from Ancient Greek διάκος (diákos) (see διάκονος (diákonos)). Parallel with Polish żak, cognate with Russian дьяк (dʹjak).
